title: India's Judoka Arun Kumar Pulled From Commonwealth Games After Failing Dope Test
excerpt: The 73 kg judo contender, seeded sixth and considered a medal hopeful, has been withdrawn from the Glasgow Games after an anti-doping violation — a fresh blow to India's reputation on the eve of the competition.
body:
• Indian judoka Arun Kumar has been withdrawn from the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow after failing a pre-competition dope test.
  • Kumar, who competes in the men's 73 kg category, was seeded sixth and trained at the Inspire Institute of Sport.
  • The withdrawal comes on the opening day of the Games and amid heightened anti-doping scrutiny of Indian athletes ahead of Glasgow 2026.
  • India had selected 14 judokas — seven men and seven women — for the Games, with judo events beginning August 1 at the SEC Centre.

Indian judoka Arun Kumar has been withdrawn from the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow after failing a pre-competition dope test, according to the Press Trust of India. The news broke on July 23 — the very day the Games officially opened — casting a shadow over India's campaign before a single bout has been fought.

Kumar, who competes in the men's 73 kg category, was seeded sixth for the event scheduled for August 1 at Glasgow's SEC Centre. He was widely considered one of India's stronger medal contenders in judo, a sport that returned to the Commonwealth programme for Glasgow after featuring in 2014 when the city last hosted the Games.

A Promising Career Derailed

Kumar was one of 21 athletes from the Inspire Institute of Sport (IIS) selected to represent India at Glasgow 2026. IIS, the high-performance centre based in Bellary, Karnataka, had been supporting his preparation across sports science, nutrition, and strength conditioning.

India had fielded a full contingent of 14 judokas — seven men and seven women — in what was expected to be one of the country's more competitive showings in the discipline. Kumar had earned his place through the final selection trials held at the K.D. Jadhav Indoor Stadium in New Delhi in February 2026.

The specifics of the substance involved and the exact timeline of the test have not been officially disclosed by either the Judo Federation of India or the Commonwealth Games Federation. The anti-doping programme for Glasgow 2026 is being administered by UK Anti-Doping (UKAD).

India's Doping Cloud Grows Darker

The withdrawal adds to a troubling pattern for Indian sports. The Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) recently reclassified India as a Category A federation — its highest-risk tier — following a surge in doping violations among Indian track and field athletes. Under the enhanced framework, Indian athletes competing in major championships are now required to undergo three out-of-competition tests within the 10 months preceding competition.

"There is a lot of focus on Indian athletics and Indian athletes at this point. I don't think anyone who could possibly be a dope offender will be coming to Glasgow. It would be a national shame."

— Adille Sumariwalla, World Athletics Vice-President and former AFI President

Sumariwalla, speaking to RevSportz ahead of the Games, had dismissed suggestions that Indian athletes were being singled out for extra testing, calling it a standard protocol for Category A federations. Kumar's withdrawal, however, undercuts those assurances and raises fresh questions about anti-doping compliance across Indian sport — not just athletics.

What It Means for India's CWG Campaign

The 2026 Commonwealth Games are already a diminished affair for India. Glasgow's slimmed-down programme features just 10 sports — down from 19 at Birmingham 2022 — with medal-rich disciplines like shooting, wrestling, badminton, cricket, and hockey all dropped as the city kept costs in check after Victoria, Australia pulled out as host.

India's 126-member squad, led by javelin star Neeraj Chopra, was banking on strong performances in athletics, weightlifting, and boxing to make up for lost ground. Judo was one of the few additional sports where India had fielded a full team across all weight categories.

With Kumar's withdrawal, India's men's 73 kg slot goes unfilled unless a late replacement is approved under the Games' athlete substitution rules. The remaining 13 Indian judokas are expected to compete as scheduled when judo events begin on July 31.

What's Next

The Judo Federation of India and the Indian Olympic Association have not yet issued formal statements on Kumar's case. A formal disciplinary proceeding is expected to follow, which could result in a multi-year ban depending on the substance and circumstances involved.

For India, the episode is a stark reminder that the country's doping problem extends beyond track and field. As Glasgow 2026 gets underway, the spotlight will be as much on India's anti-doping credibility as on its medal prospects.
